title: Mobility
subtitle: Build usable movement for daily tasks, exercise, and long-term function

blocks.text: This lesson is general education, not diagnosis, treatment or rehab. Fill out CSEP’s Get Active Questionnaire before a big increase in activity and follow what it says. Get qualified advice for a recent injury or surgery, repeated falls, a joint that gives way, pain you can’t explain, numbness or weakness, or a health condition that changes how you move. Stop and get urgent medical help for chest pressure or pain, fainting, severe or unusual shortness of breath, sudden nerve symptoms, a serious fall, or suddenly being unable to put weight on a leg.
You’ll link one useful task to four ingredients: range, control, strength and confidence. Mobility is movement you can use, not a contest to see whose hip can produce the most surprising geometry.
Move through your day with less stiffness and more ease.
blocks.detail: Mobility built around a real task, like getting up off the floor, improves the movements you use every day.
blocks.extra: Section 03 shows how to find what’s limiting a movement.

sections.title: Define Mobility by What It Lets You Do

blocks.text: Mobility is moving a joint or body part through a usable range, with control. It helps you reach, turn, squat, walk, get dressed, drive, work and exercise.

Flexibility is one part of mobility. A muscle may allow a big range, but you may lack the strength or control to use it. Someone else may have enough range for every task that matters without looking especially flexible.

Start with a task. “Reach the top shelf without leaning” is more useful than “improve shoulder mobility.” “Walk downstairs comfortably” is more useful than “fix my ankles.” The task shows which movement matters.
Notice how the real movement feels before you choose an exercise. Mobility drills should serve the task, not pile up in a folder like coupons you never use.

items.title: “More range of motion is always better.”
items.text: Useful range depends on the person and the task. Extra range without control or stability may not help, or may even get in the way.

blocks.text: Choose one movement problem
Finish this sentence: “I want enough controlled movement to ___ more comfortably.”

Most tasks use several body parts. A squat uses the ankles, knees, hips and trunk. Reaching overhead uses the shoulder, shoulder blade, upper back and ribs. Turning to back up a car uses the neck, upper back, trunk, eyes and seat position.

Watch where the movement first changes. Does your heel lift? Does your back arch? Does one side move differently? Does the task feel blocked, weak, wobbly or painful? Watching tells you where to start, but it doesn’t diagnose the cause.
Change the setup and test again. Raise the chair, go less deep, stand closer to the shelf or use support. If the task improves, you’ve found a useful change to use while your capacity builds.
The first heel lift, shoulder shrug, twist or wobble often shows where the task goes past what you can do right now.

sections.title: Use Active Movement Before Forcing Range

blocks.text: Active mobility uses your own muscles to move and control a joint. Examples include ankle rocks, controlled knee lifts, shoulder circles, upper-back turns and a slow sit-to-stand through a comfortable range.

Start with a small, smooth range. Breathe normally. Repeat a few controlled moves and notice whether the range gets easier. A mild feeling of effort or stretch is fine. Sharp pain, catching, a joint giving way or nerve symptoms are not training targets.
Active movement shows whether you can control the range you have. It also gets your body ready for related activity. The exercise should look like practice, not a negotiation with a stubborn hinge.

items.title: “Mobility work must feel intense to create change.”
items.text: Gentle, repeated movement linked to a real task can improve comfort, coordination and usable range without strong discomfort.

blocks.text: A simple starting dose: 2 or 3 sets of 5 to 10 slow, controlled reps, most days of the week. Mobility responds to frequent, short practice better than one long session. Test your chosen task again every two weeks.
The edge of your usable range is the point where control starts to slip. Instead of forcing farther, pause in a comfortable position and practise holding your alignment and breathing.

For an ankle, this might be moving your knee forward with support while your heel stays down. For a shoulder, it might be lifting your arm only as high as your ribs and shoulder blade stay in control. For the hip, it might be a slow step or a supported split stance.
Use support when balance is part of the challenge. Shrink the range if your speed, breathing or position changes. Control turns the motion you have into mobility you can rely on.
A smaller range you can control is more useful than a larger range borrowed from momentum.
Mobility often improves when strength improves. If you can reach a position but can’t push or absorb force there, your body may avoid it during real tasks.

Pair a mobility drill with a related strength move. An ankle rock pairs with a supported calf raise or step. A controlled overhead reach pairs with a suitable press or pull. A hip move pairs with a chair rise, bridge, hinge or step.
Use a resistance and range you can manage. Progress one thing at a time. The goal isn’t to do a mobility ritual and then forget the range exists. Give your body a job there.

items.title: “Tightness always means a muscle needs stretching.”
items.text: A tight feeling can come from tiredness, weakness, new activity, pain sensitivity, joint limits, an irritated nerve or protective tension. The right response depends on the cause.

blocks.text: Noor solves the floor problem
paragraphs: Noor, 38, lived in Edmonton and wanted to sit on the floor with her kids and get back up without grabbing the coffee table. She downloaded a long hip-mobility routine and did it now and then. It was full of poses with names that sounded like international airports. Getting up off the floor didn’t change.

One Saturday, after a puzzle with her daughter, she hauled herself up using both hands and the table, and felt embarrassed. She was tempted to buy an even longer program. Instead, she decided to test the actual task and find out what was going wrong.

Lowering herself down felt controlled. Getting up was the problem: it took momentum and both hands. Her ankles and hips had enough range for a higher seat. Leg strength and confidence were the bigger limits.

Noor practised a supported half-kneeling move beside a sturdy chair. She used a cushion to shorten the distance, added chair rises and supported split squats twice a week, and finished with gentle ankle and hip moves.
Every two weeks, she tested getting up from the floor. Slowly she used a lower cushion and less hand support. One week the cushion went missing under a pile of toys, and she found she didn’t need it.
After eight weeks, she could stand up using one hand and a controlled step. Her hips hadn’t become circus performers. They had become useful, and the coffee table went back to holding coffee.

blocks.text: A mobility plan earns its place when reaching, turning, squatting, stepping or another chosen movement gets better.
Test the real task, and you’ll know exactly what to work on.
blocks.detail: Finding the true limit, whether it’s range, strength or confidence, turns scattered drills into steady progress.
blocks.extra: Section 08 shows where to fit mobility into your day.

blocks.text: Before exercise, use controlled moves that look like the activity ahead. Start easy, then slowly add range or pace. Between long stretches of sitting, short movement breaks can bring back comfort and variety.
After activity, use gentle movement if it feels good. Longer stretching can be a separate session when flexibility is your real goal. Mobility doesn’t need a thirty-minute ceremony before every walk.

A focused routine might use two or three moves for your chosen task. Practise often enough to learn them, then test the task again. If nothing changes, rethink the exercise, the dose or your first guess about the cause.

sections.title: Read the Response and Change One Feature

blocks.text: Repeat the same small routine until it feels familiar. Then add a little range, hold time, resistance, reps or task difficulty. Change one thing and check how you feel later that day and the next morning.

Stop and get checked for a sudden loss of movement, a joint that locks after an injury, a lot of swelling, suddenly being unable to put weight on a leg, weakness that keeps getting worse, numbness, or pain that’s severe or worsening. This paragraph has no humour, because these signs need clear care decisions.

items.title: “A joint must move symmetrically on both sides.”
items.text: Some differences are normal because of your build, history, handedness, sport, work or past surgery. What matters is how well you function, your control, your symptoms and advice from a professional.

blocks.text: Two focused moves practised often can beat twelve random drills visited once in a burst of optimism.

Mobility help may be available through physiotherapy, occupational therapy, community health centres, rehab programs, rec centres, Indigenous health organizations, campuses and adapted exercise services. Coverage, referrals, regulation, eligibility and wait times vary by province and territory.
CSEP professionals can guide your exercise within their training. Physiotherapists assess and treat movement problems. Occupational therapists help you adapt tasks and spaces for daily life.
Key takeaway
Mobility is usable, controlled movement. Start with a task that matters, find where the movement breaks down, practise active range, strengthen it and test the task again before adding more drills.
If you’re comfortable with it, film one normal rep from a safe angle. Ten seconds can reveal a heel lift or shoulder shrug that your internal camera crew forgot to report.

items.title: How does mobility differ from flexibility?
items.detail: Mobility is usable movement with control; flexibility describes available range or tissue tolerance.

items.title: What four ingredients make up the Movement Problem Solver?
items.detail: Available range, control, strength, and confidence.

items.title: Why should a learner test the real task first?
items.detail: It identifies the meaningful problem and provides a result to compare later.

items.title: What is active mobility?
items.detail: Moving a joint through a range using your own muscles and control.

items.title: Why can a smaller controlled range be useful?
items.detail: It allows dependable position, balance, and breathing while capacity develops.

items.title: What limited Noor's floor transfer most?
items.detail: Leg strength, task control, and confidence were larger limits than hip range.

items.title: Why pair mobility with strength?
items.detail: Strength helps produce and absorb force in the newly available range.

items.title: Name two signs that require assessment.
items.detail: Sudden movement loss, marked swelling, inability to bear weight, worsening pain, weakness, or numbness.

items.title: Active mobility
items.text: Controlled movement produced by the person's own muscles.

items.title: Compensation
items.text: A change elsewhere in the body used to complete a movement.

items.title: Mobility
items.text: The ability to move through a usable range with control.

items.title: Range of motion
items.text: The amount of movement available at a joint or body region.

items.title: Task modification
items.text: A change to setup, support, height, load, or position that makes a task manageable.
